section.title: The Seven Bowls of Wrath
section.sectionRationale: The seven bowls are the third and final septet of judgment in Revelation, after the seals and trumpets, a self-contained unit bounded by the command in 16:1 and the seventh bowl's completed cry in 16:17-21. It deliberately echoes the plagues of Exodus and climaxes in the naming of Armageddon and God's remembering of Babylon the great, which the next two chapters unfold at length.
section.thesis: In the seven bowls God empties out, at last, the full and undiluted measure of His wrath on a world that has hardened itself against Him; sores, blood, fire, darkness, and earthquake fall in relentless succession, yet impenitent hearts curse rather than repent, until the final bowl declares it is done and sets the stage for Babylon's fall.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the command to pour out wrath; the first three bowls turning creation itself, land, sea, and rivers, against a world that shed the saints' blood; the fourth and fifth bowls of scorching sun and darkened throne, met by defiant refusal to repent; the sixth bowl drying the Euphrates and gathering the kings for Armageddon; and the seventh bowl's completed cry, unleashing the great earthquake and the remembering of Babylon.

units.label: The command to pour out wrath
units.note: seven angels sent from the temple

verses.text: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels, “Go, pour out on the earth the seven {{phiale|bowls}} of God's {{thymos|wrath}}.”

units.label: The first three bowls: sores, sea, and rivers of blood
units.note: creation itself turns on a world that shed the saints' blood

verses.text: So the first angel went and {{ekcheo|poured out}} his bowl on the earth, and loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
And the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it turned to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.
And the third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and springs of water, and they turned to blood.
And I heard the angel of the waters say: “Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was, because You have brought these judgments.
For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.”
And I heard the altar reply: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.”

units.label: The fourth and fifth bowls: scorching sun and darkened throne

verses.text: Then the fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was given power to scorch the people with fire.
And the people were scorched by intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues; yet they did not {{metanoeo|repent}} and give Him glory.
And the fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and men began to gnaw their tongues in anguish
and curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores; yet they did not repent of their deeds.

units.label: The sixth bowl: Euphrates dried up and Armageddon gathered
units.note: demonic spirits assemble the kings for battle

verses.text: And the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.
And I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet.
These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
“Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who {{gregoreo|remains awake}} and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.”
And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called {{har_magedon|Armageddon}}.

units.label: The seventh bowl: it is done
units.note: earthquake, hail, and the remembering of Babylon

verses.text: Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, “{{gegonen|It is done}}!”
And there were flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder, and a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth, so mighty was the great quake.
The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed. And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His {{thymos|wrath}}.
Then every island fled, and no mountain could be found.
And great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above. And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.

phiale.gloss: A shallow, wide bowl used for pouring out liquid offerings. In Revelation the seven phialai are not vessels of blessing but of judgment, poured out in rapid succession like the plagues of Exodus. Where the earlier trumpets brought partial judgment, the bowls are total, each emptied completely, picturing wrath with nothing held back.

thymos.gloss: Hot, intense passion, often paired with orge, God's settled and considered wrath, to describe the full weight of divine anger. In 16:19 the two words combine, the wine of the thymos of His orge, doubling the force of the phrase. It names God's holy, right anger against evil, not arbitrary rage but the just response of a righteous Judge.

ekcheo.gloss: To pour out, to spill. The verb is used repeatedly of the angels emptying their bowls, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for outpoured plagues and, in Joel and Acts, for the outpouring of the Spirit. Here the same verb pictures total, decisive outpouring, wrath given no half measure.

metanoeo.gloss: To change one's mind, to repent. Revelation's plague narrative is marked by a grim refrain, that those under judgment cursed God, yet they did not repent. Its repetition across the chapter shows that judgment alone, however severe, does not produce repentance apart from grace; hardened hearts curse rather than turn.

gregoreo.gloss: To stay awake, to be watchful and alert. Set within the plague narrative, the beatitude of verse 15 calls for readiness, not speculation about timing, echoing Jesus' own repeated call in the Gospels to stay awake for His unannounced coming. It commends a life clothed and ready rather than caught exposed and ashamed.

har_magedon.gloss: A Greek transliteration of a Hebrew phrase, which the text itself flags as Hebrew. Most read it as Har Megiddo, the hill country of Megiddo, an ancient battlefield in Israel's history; others propose different derivations or a symbolic, non-geographic sense. Whatever its precise root, John names it the place of final gathering for battle against God, deliberately drawing on Israel's memory of decisive battles.

gegonen.gloss: The perfect tense of ginomai, to happen or become, here meaning it has happened, it is done, it stands accomplished. The perfect tense marks a completed action with continuing effect. The same word closes God's redemptive purposes at the new creation, Revelation 21:6, so its use here for the completion of judgment anticipates its later use for the completion of salvation, both spoken by the same declaring voice.

basic.context: This chapter closes out Revelation's three cycles of judgment, seals, trumpets, and now bowls. An angel commands seven angels to empty bowls of God's wrath on the earth, and one by one the world that worships the beast is struck: sores, blood-red seas and rivers, scorching sun, darkness, a dried-up Euphrates, and a shattering earthquake. Even under such judgment, people curse God rather than turn to Him, and the chapter ends by gathering armies at Armageddon and naming Babylon, whose fall the next chapters describe.
basic.hermeneutics: Readers disagree on how literally to take the plagues and on when and how Armageddon happens, whether as a single future battle, a symbol of history's constant conflict, or events already fulfilled in some sense in the first centuries. What is not disputed is the pattern: God's judgment on organized evil is real, complete, and just, and it is followed immediately by an unrepentant refrain, showing that hearts set against God do not soften under judgment alone.
basic.originalLanguages: The bowls are phialai, wide vessels emptied completely, unlike the partial judgments of the trumpets. Wrath is thymos, God's hot, right anger, doubled with orge at the chapter's climax. Twice the text notes that people did not metanoeo, repent, even under plague. And the gathering place is Har Magedon, a Hebrew name whose exact meaning is debated but whose Old Testament echoes of decisive battle are unmistakable.
basic.typology: The bowls deliberately recall the plagues God sent on Egypt, boils, blood, and darkness, showing that the exodus pattern, judgment on oppressors and deliverance for God's people, reaches its final form here. The completed cry it is done anticipates the same word spoken over the finished new creation in chapter 21.
basic.christ: The bowls are called the wrath of God, but this is the same God whose wrath the Lamb absorbed at the cross for those who trust Him; those united to Christ do not face this judgment, which falls only on those who bear the beast's mark and refuse to repent. The Lamb who was slain is also the Lord who commands the temple's angels and finishes the judgment.
basic.god: God is patient and just: even now He is called Holy One, righteous, and true, and the altar itself testifies that His judgments are deserved. Yet He is also the one who limits and completes judgment precisely, on His own timetable, never one bowl too many or too few.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 7-11 supplies the pattern of plagues on a hard-hearted oppressor. Isaiah 34 and Jeremiah 50-51 supply the Babylon judgment language that Revelation 16-18 draws on. Joel 3 and Zechariah 12 supply the picture of nations gathered for a final battle near Israel.
basic.oneStory: The bowls show that God's patience with organized evil is not endless; a day comes when wrath is poured out fully and finally. But this same chapter's altar cries that His judgments are true and just, precisely because at the cross Jesus already bore the wrath His people deserved, so that all who trust Him are kept from this hour and instead wait for Babylon's fall and the marriage of the Lamb.

context.literary:
Chapter 16 is built as a series of seven acts, but its shape is more interesting than a list. The first four bowls strike the four spheres of the created order in a fixed sequence: earth, sea, rivers and springs, and sun. The pattern is the same as the first four trumpets in 8:7 to 12, where earth, sea, rivers and heavenly lights were struck. The fifth bowl falls on a throne, not on nature, and the sixth and seventh move toward the battle and the end. John breaks the series twice. After the third bowl he hears a voice of justification from the angel of the waters and the altar, verses 5 to 7. After the sixth he hears the Lord Himself say, 'Behold, I am coming like a thief,' verse 15, a sudden aside in the first person that has no seventh part to answer it.

The chapter's refrain is the refusal to repent. Verses 9, 11 and 21 end in the same way: people cursed God. They do not turn, even when the judgment is plain. This repeated failure holds the sequence together and explains why the bowls fall as they do. The seventh bowl is the longest and the climax. It delivers the cry 'It is done!' from the throne, then the earthquake, the splitting of the great city into three parts, the remembering of Babylon, the disappearance of islands and mountains, and the great hail. The last verse is a sentence that ends with an act of cursing. The chapter is shaped so that the reader sees both the reach of God's judgment and the hardness of hearts that will not give way.
context.historical:
The first hearers knew the Exodus plagues, and the bowls are written to echo them. The sores, the water turned to blood, the frogs, the darkness and the hail were all part of the story told at every Passover. The effect is to cast the beast's empire as a new Pharaoh and God's coming action as a new deliverance. John's readers in Roman Asia lived under a power that boasted of its own permanence, and the scene is built to say that Rome's claim, or any similar claim, is a claim that God will not leave standing.

The Euphrates had a particular meaning. It was the river that marked the eastern edge of the lands of the Bible, and invading armies from Assyria and Babylon had come across it. It was also, in John's own time, the frontier between the Roman Empire and the Parthians, who were feared as an army from the East. The drying of the river calls on both memories. Isaiah 44:27 speaks of the Lord saying to the deep, 'Be dry,' in the context of Cyrus, who took Babylon after its river defences were turned, and Jeremiah 51:36 speaks of God drying up Babylon's sea. The Plain of Megiddo, which lies behind the name Armageddon, was the most famous battlefield of the land: Barak and Sisera fought there, Judges 5:19, and Josiah died there, 2 Kings 23:29. A reader who knew the Scriptures would hear it as the place where kings had gathered, and fallen.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on the plagues of Exodus, Psalm 79:6 and Jeremiah 10:25 for the language of pouring out wrath, Isaiah 34 and Jeremiah 50 and 51 for the judgment of Babylon, and Daniel 12:1 for the unparalleled distress. The prophets had already spoken of nations gathered for a final battle, Joel 3:2 and Zechariah 12:11 to 14:2, and John gives that gathering a name. The appearance of the demonic frogs from the mouth of the dragon, beast and false prophet looks back to 12:3, 13:1 and 13:11, and to the plague of frogs in Exodus 8. Elsewhere in Revelation, 'Behold, I am coming like a thief' repeats Jesus' own words in 3:3, which in turn recall Matthew 24:43 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2.

The chapter also leads forward. 'It is done!' has an echo in 21:6, where the same word is spoken from the throne at the beginning of the new creation, which suggests that the wrath's completion and the new creation's beginning belong together. The 'remembering' of Babylon, verse 19, is the opposite of God's remembering of Noah in Genesis 8:1 and of Israel in Exodus 2:24. Chapters 17 and 18 will take up the thread, explaining who Babylon is and why her fall brings lament from some and rejoicing in heaven from others. The splitting of the great city is also contrasted with the city that comes down from heaven in 21:2, a city which cannot be shaken.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote the bowls so that his readers would see judgment as just, complete and certain, and not as random catastrophe. The song of the angel of the waters says that those who spilled the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink, 'as they deserve.' The altar answers with its own confirmation. These interruptions are not decoration. They tell the churches that every plague has a reason that can be said aloud before the throne, and the reason is the faithful blood that has been shed.

He also meant the hearers to take a warning from the hearts in the chapter. Three times the stricken curse God and refuse to repent. That is not a prediction of what everyone will do but an account of what the beast's followers do, and it makes plain that there is a kind of resistance that suffering by itself does not heal. The aside of verse 15 turns the warning into an invitation to the reader: stay awake, stay clothed. The churches in Sardis and Laodicea had heard something like that already in 3:3 and 3:18.

And he meant the end to be comforting for those who had been wronged. The great city splits and Babylon is remembered. The reader is told that whatever empire seems to hold the world, there is a day on which God remembers what it has done.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The bowls are described and not commanded. The only direct instruction is the voice from heaven in verse 15, 'Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.' That is a word to the reader, and it is a prescription to be watchful and to hold on to the righteousness one has been given. Everything else is the report of a vision.

It follows that the chapter should not be turned into a recipe for how believers should treat unbelievers. The angel of the waters praises God's justice, and the saints do not execute it. The New Testament says that vengeance belongs to the Lord, Romans 12:19, and that Christians are to feed an enemy and overcome evil with good, Romans 12:20 to 21. The chapter should also not be used to calculate the date of the end, since Jesus said no one knows the day or hour, Matthew 24:36, and verse 15 stresses surprise.

What it does shape is the believer's imagination. When injustice seems unanswered, the chapter shows the answer being prepared. When people do not repent in the face of obvious signs, the chapter explains that not every hard heart is changed by pressure. It teaches the church to pray for repentance while it still can, and to keep its own garments.

debates.question: Are the bowls literal events, or symbols?

views.label: Literal future events
views.case: The plagues are described in physical terms, sores, blood, scorching, darkness, a drying river, an earthquake, hail of a stated weight, and the Exodus plagues on which they are modelled were physical. The 'almost a hundred pounds' of hail in verse 21 reads like measurement. On this view God will bring about such events at the end of the age.

views.label: Symbolic pictures of divine judgment
views.case: Revelation is introduced as something 'made known' by signs in 1:1, and numbers and images throughout are symbolic. The bowls are said to pour on a throne and into the air. The pictures are taken from Exodus and the prophets so that they will be heard as pictures of God's judgment on a system, not as a forecast of each event.

views.label: Both, with the literal rooted in symbolic frames
views.case: Some hold that real events may stand behind images chosen for their Old Testament associations. Exodus itself had real plagues that also carried theological meaning, and the bowls may be a mixture of actual calamity and scriptural patterning.

debates.bearing: All readings share the point that creation itself serves God's verdict, that the judgment is just and total, and that suffering alone does not bring repentance. The literal or symbolic decision should be made on the whole book and held with humility.

debates.question: What is Armageddon?

views.label: A future literal battle
views.case: The text says kings are assembled 'for battle on the great day of God the Almighty,' and names a place. Joel 3 and Zechariah 14 also speak of nations gathered against Jerusalem. Many therefore expect a final military conflict in the region.

views.label: A symbol of the final conflict between God and evil
views.case: There is no mountain at Megiddo, only a plain, so the name does not describe a literal site. The place name stands for every earlier battlefield in which God's enemies gathered and were destroyed. Revelation 19:19 to 21 shows the battle won by the word from the Rider's mouth, not by armies, which suggests that it is a theological conflict.

views.label: Already fulfilled in the first century
views.case: Some preterist readers connect the kings of the East and the gathering to events around Rome in the late first century, and see the bowls as God's judgment on the empire and on Jerusalem within the history that John's readers would soon live through.

debates.bearing: The text's own emphasis is that the gathering is God's doing and that the outcome has been announced, since the angels at the altar have already said that His judgments are true and just. The location and timing matter less than the fact that the kings are drawn into an end they cannot win.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in the Greek explain the force of the chapter. The command in verse 1, 'pour out,' uses the verb ekcheo, which the Greek Old Testament uses when God's wrath is poured out on the nations, as in Psalm 79:6. It is the verb of liquid emptied from a vessel, and it fits the bowls well. It is the same verb that Paul uses for the Spirit being poured out in Titus 3:6, so the same image of emptying a vessel serves blessing and judgment alike.

The first bowl brings 'loathsome, malignant sores,' and the Greek noun is helkos, the word the Greek translation of Exodus uses for the boils that broke out on the Egyptians, Exodus 9:9 to 11. Even the adjectives, kakon and poneron, mean bad and evil, so the sores are described morally as well as physically. The sixth bowl leaves the plagues of Egypt and turns to a different sort of word: 'the kings of the East' are, literally, the kings 'from the rising of the sun,' a phrase that speaks of the direction of dawn.

The word translated 'cursed' in verses 9, 11 and 21 is blasphemeo, to blaspheme, and the repetition is a deliberate hammering. The same verb describes what the beast does in 13:6. The verse 9 also contains the phrase 'give Him glory,' doxa, the glory the angel commanded in 14:7. The call that went out with the gospel is thus the very thing that is refused when judgment arrives, and the repetition shows that the failure is wilful.

The seventh bowl is poured 'into the air,' aer. In Ephesians 2:2 Paul speaks of the ruler of the kingdom of the air, and the placement suggests that the last bowl strikes the sphere in which the enemy's power is thought to operate. The cry 'It is done!' is gegonen, in the perfect tense, which describes a completed event whose result stands. Revelation 21:6 uses the same perfect, in the plural, gegonan, when the new creation is announced. In verse 21 the hail weighs 'almost a hundred pounds,' which translates the adjective talantiaios, the weight of a talent, a standard measure of heavy loads. English readers should not hear a precise laboratory figure in it, only the shock of ice falling in stones the size of a man's burden.

typology.fulfillment: The sores, blood, frogs, darkness and hail correspond to five of the plagues in Exodus 7 to 10. Pharaoh's hardness of heart there, 'he would not listen,' Exodus 8:15, corresponds to the stricken who 'did not repent' here. The escalation is that Exodus struck one land while the bowls strike the whole earth, and where Egypt's plagues led to a rescue, these lead to the end of the age. The type falls short in that Egypt's plagues ended in the rescue of a people, while these end the age itself.

The ancient city of Babylon stood on the Euphrates and trusted the river as a defence. Isaiah 44:27 and Jeremiah 50:38 and 51:36 speak of the Lord drying up its waters, and Daniel 5 shows the city falling in a night. In Revelation 16:12 the river dries to make a road for kings, and the city in verse 19 is remembered. The new Babylon, the world system of chapters 17 and 18, falls in the same manner. The correspondence is limited, because the ancient city fell to a human conqueror, while the final one falls to God's direct action.

Jesus said that if the owner of the house had known when the thief was coming he would have stayed awake, Matthew 24:43. Paul told the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord comes like a thief, 1 Thessalonians 5:2, and Jesus told Sardis the same in Revelation 3:3. In 16:15 the picture is joined to clothing, 'clothed, so that he will not go naked,' which recalls the white garments Laodicea was counselled to buy, 3:18. The correspondence is of surprise and of readiness. It falls short in that a thief takes, whereas the Lord comes to judge and to reward.

typology.type: The altar and the blood of the saints
typology.fulfillment: In 6:9 to 10 the souls under the altar cry out, 'How long?' for their blood to be avenged. In 16:6 to 7 the altar speaks, and the answer is that those who shed that blood are given blood to drink. This echoes Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out from the ground, and Exodus 7, where the Nile's water becomes blood. The escalation is from one man's blood to the blood of saints and prophets, and from one river to all the waters. The type is limited because the justice is exact, not bloodthirsty, and the saints themselves are not the executioners.

study.christ:
A chapter about bowls of wrath might seem the least likely place to look for Christ, but the New Testament helps us see that He stands behind it in three ways. The first is that the judgments are described as true and just, and Jesus said that the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. The voice from the temple in verse 1 and the voice from the throne in verse 17 speak with God's authority, and in this book the throne is shared by God and the Lamb, 22:1. The one who is coming 'like a thief' in verse 15 is the speaker of 3:3 and so is Christ Himself, who interrupts the angels' work to address the reader. In the middle of the bowls the Lord of the church says, in the first person, that He is coming, and He pronounces a blessing.

The second way is the absence of any bowl on those who belong to Him. The first bowl falls on 'those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image,' and the later bowls fall on the beast's throne and its kingdom. Those who belong to the Lamb have the Lamb's name on their foreheads, 14:1, and have already been placed beside the sea of glass, 15:2. Paul states what this means: 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1, and 'we will be saved from God's wrath through Him,' Romans 5:9. The cross stands between believers and the cup, since Jesus Himself asked that this cup be taken from Him and then drank it, Matthew 26:39.

The third way is the angel's phrase 'who is and was,' addressed to God in verse 5. The usual third part, 'who is to come,' is absent, because He has already come. That is a quiet sign that the end has arrived by the time of the seventh bowl. And the cry 'It is done!' from the throne evokes the cry from the cross, 'It is finished,' John 19:30, and anticipates the same declaration at the new creation in 21:6. We should not claim too much from the verbal link, because the Greek words are different. But the shape is the same: a word that closes the work. At Calvary it closed the work of atonement, at the throne it closes the work of judgment, and in the new creation it opens the world to come.

The chapter does not allow believers to treat judgment lightly. The call of verse 15 is addressed to them: stay awake, stay clothed. The garment is the righteousness of Christ, which Revelation 19:8 says is given to His bride.
study.god:
The doctrine of God in this chapter is at its starkest. He is called by two titles, 'Holy One, who is and was,' and 'Lord God Almighty.' The angel of the waters does not say that God has become angry. He says that God is righteous because He has brought these judgments, and the reason is given: they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets. God's justice here is retributive in the exact sense. The punishment is shaped by the crime, blood for blood, and it is just because it is deserved. The altar confirms it in words that repeat the earlier hymn of 15:3, 'true and just.'

The chapter also shows God's authority over creation. Every sphere, land, sea, river, sun, air, and every force, hail, darkness, earthquake, answers to His command. The plague of the sun in verse 9 comes from a God 'who had authority over these plagues,' a phrase that says He rules the very things on which life depends. It also shows His power over the demonic. The three unclean spirits go out to the kings, but only to assemble them for 'the great day of God the Almighty.' Evil's most elaborate scheme is set to serve His day.

Another feature is His restraint. After three cycles of judgment He still speaks to the reader with a blessing, and the long refusals to repent show that He has not forced hearts. God's patience and God's judgment are not in conflict here, because the judgment comes after the patience has been refused, and because the people are pictured as rejecting Him to the end. That does not make God less sovereign. The text says that He gave them blood to drink, and that it was 'given' to the sun to scorch, using the passive verbs that reflect heaven's rule.

The chapter closes with His remembering. God remembered Babylon, and the wine of the fury of His wrath is the cup she is given. In Scripture, God's remembering is always a decisive act. He remembers Noah, Abraham and Israel for rescue, and He remembers Babylon for judgment. It shows a God who does not forget, who keeps account of blood and of prayer. For worship, the right response is the one the altar gives: to agree with God that His judgments are true and just, and to keep one's garments clean while the day approaches.

crossReferences.note: The plague of boils in Egypt, from which the first bowl takes its sores. The Greek word is the same in the Greek Old Testament. The link marks the first bowl as an Exodus judgment, falling on people who have chosen the beast's side as Egypt chose Pharaoh's.

The Nile turns to blood and the fish die. The second and third bowls reproduce this on the sea and on all fresh water. In Exodus the plague was a sign aimed at Egypt's gods, and in Revelation it is aimed at the world that has trusted in the beast.

The first four trumpets also struck earth, sea, rivers and the lights of heaven, but only by a third. Setting the two lists together shows what 'final' means: the same pattern, now complete and without limit.
The souls under the altar ask how long it will be before their blood is avenged. In 16:5 to 7 the altar itself answers. The prayer of the martyrs finds its reply in the justice of the bowls.

The Lord says to the deep, 'Be dry,' and speaks it in the context of Cyrus, who took Babylon. John uses the drying of the Euphrates to say that the defence of the great city fails at God's word, and a road is opened for kings.

Kings fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, and took no plunder. The old battlefield behind the name Armageddon was a place where kings gathered and gained nothing. The echo prepares the reader for the result of the gathering in verse 16.

The mourning in the plain of Megiddo is used by Zechariah as the measure of Jerusalem's grief over the pierced one. Armageddon is a place where grief and judgment meet, and the prophetic background shows that the final gathering concerns Israel's God and His Messiah.

Jesus tells Sardis that He will come like a thief if they do not wake up. In 16:15 He says the same to the whole church, in the middle of the bowls. The warning is repeated because it is the one need that the judgments cannot do for the reader.

Laodicea is counselled to buy white garments so that the shame of nakedness is not exposed. Revelation 16:15 repeats the shame of nakedness. The two verses explain each other: the clothing is the righteousness that Christ provides.

'It is done!' is spoken again from the throne at the beginning of the new creation. The word in 16:17 closes the age of wrath, and the same word in 21:6 opens the age of the water of life, so the two verses frame the whole judgment as the doorway to the world made new.

study.oneStory:
The story that begins with 'it was very good' in Genesis 1 turns on a pattern of patience and judgment. God warns, God waits, God acts. He warned Cain that sin crouched at the door, and Abel's blood cried out from the ground, Genesis 4:7 and 4:10. He waited through the long building of the ark in the days of Noah. He sent ten plagues on Egypt and let Pharaoh harden his heart. He let Babylon take Jerusalem and then let Babylon fall. The bowls are the last of these in the telling, and they gather every earlier act into one. When the angel of the waters says that those who spilled the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink, he is closing a ledger that was opened with Abel.

The chapter also holds one of the Bible's most sober insights, that judgment alone does not turn hearts. In Exodus, Pharaoh's heart hardened under each plague, and in Revelation 16 people curse God as they are struck. The same Scripture insists that repentance is the gift of God, Acts 11:18 and 2 Timothy 2:25, and it never says that suffering produces it by itself. That is why the story needs a Saviour and not only a judge. What changes hearts is the cross, the kindness of God, Romans 2:4, and the Spirit.

Looking forward, the bowls open onto Babylon's explanation in chapter 17 and her fall in chapter 18, and then to the return of the King in chapter 19. The 'great day of God the Almighty' in 16:14 is the day toward which Joel, Zephaniah and Zechariah looked. The completed 'It is done!' of 16:17 answers the 'It is finished' of the cross and ushers in the declaration of 21:6. The islands that flee and the mountains that vanish remind us that the old order cannot remain, and that what follows is not a patched world but a new one: a new heaven and earth in which the sea is gone, death is gone, and nothing accursed remains, 21:1 and 22:3. The wrath of chapter 16 is the last hard act that makes that gentleness possible.

quiz.q: What do the seven bowls represent in Revelation 16?

options.text: The full and final outpouring of God's wrath on the world that worships the beast, poured out completely rather than partially.
options.note: The bowls follow the seals and trumpets as the last and most total of Revelation's judgment cycles.

options.text: A partial warning judgment meant only to call people to repentance, like the trumpets before them.
options.note: The bowls are total, not partial; the chapter stresses their completeness.

options.text: Blessings poured out on the faithful during the tribulation.
options.note: The bowls are judgments on those who bear the mark of the beast, not blessings.

options.text: A literal set of kitchen vessels used in the Jerusalem temple with no symbolic meaning.
options.note: The bowls are symbolic vessels of wrath, not literal temple furniture.

quiz.q: What refrain appears repeatedly after the plagues fall on people?

options.text: They cursed God but did not repent, showing that judgment alone does not soften a hardened heart.
options.note: Revelation 16:9 and 16:11 both record this impenitence refrain.

options.text: They immediately repented and turned to God in large numbers.
options.note: The opposite is stated twice in the chapter.

options.text: They blamed the beast for the plagues rather than God.
options.note: The text says they cursed the name of God directly.

options.text: They were unaffected and continued life as normal.
options.note: The plagues caused real suffering, sores, heat, and anguish.

quiz.q: What happens at the sixth bowl?

options.text: The Euphrates is dried up to prepare the way for kings, and demonic spirits gather earth's rulers for battle at Armageddon.
options.note: Revelation 16:12-16 describes the sixth bowl and the gathering at Armageddon.

options.text: The sun is given power to scorch people with fire.
options.note: That is the fourth bowl, not the sixth.

options.text: The sea turns to blood and every living thing in it dies.
options.note: That is the second bowl.

options.text: The throne of the beast is plunged into darkness.
options.note: That is the fifth bowl.

quiz.q: What does the seventh bowl declare, and what follows?

options.text: It is done, followed by lightning, thunder, the greatest earthquake in human history, and the remembering of Babylon the great.
options.note: Revelation 16:17-19 describes this climactic sequence.

options.text: It is done, followed immediately by the wedding of the Lamb.
options.note: The wedding of the Lamb comes later, after Babylon's fall in chapters 17-19, not immediately here.

options.text: Come up here, calling John into heaven for a new vision.
options.note: That call happens elsewhere in Revelation, not at the seventh bowl.

options.text: Repent, for the kingdom is at hand, a call to national Israel.
options.note: The seventh bowl declares completion, not a call to repentance.

quiz.q: Why do the angel of the waters and the altar both speak in this chapter?

options.text: To declare that God's judgments are righteous, true, and deserved, since the world had spilled the blood of saints and prophets.
options.note: Revelation 16:5-7 records both voices affirming God's justice.

options.text: To beg God to stop the plagues out of pity for the wicked.
options.note: Both voices affirm the justice of the judgments rather than pleading against them.

options.text: To announce the arrival of the beast's kingdom.
options.note: They speak of God's judgments, not the beast's arrival.

options.text: To argue that the judgments are excessive and unjust.
options.note: They declare the opposite, that the judgments are true and just.

questions: The bowls fall on a world that curses God rather than turns to Him, even under judgment. Is there an area of your own life where you've grown hardened rather than repentant when things go wrong?

The angel of the waters and the altar both insist that God's judgments are true and just. When you can't make sense of suffering or judgment in the world, how does trusting God's justice, even before you understand it, steady you?
Armageddon is described as a gathering for a battle whose outcome God has already determined. Where in your life do you need to trust that the outcome, not just the process, belongs to God?
The chapter closes with it is done, echoing the finished work of the cross. How does knowing that Christ has already borne God's wrath for you change how you face this passage's severity?
This chapter warns that people can curse God under judgment rather than repent. What helps you turn toward God, rather than away from Him, when life is hard?

translationNotes.note: Har Magedon, Armageddon, is explicitly flagged by John as a Hebrew name; its exact derivation and geography are debated, most commonly linked to Megiddo, though no mountain by that name exists there, so some read it as a symbolic rather than strictly literal location.
The refrain yet they did not repent translates metanoeo, and its repetition across the chapter is a deliberate structural device, not incidental detail, underscoring hardened impenitence.

The fury of the wine of the wrath renders a doubled Greek phrase, thymos and orge together, a construction translators render variously, fury of his wrath, fierceness of his wrath, to capture the intensifying effect of stacking two wrath-words.
Bowls, phialai, are broad, shallow vessels for pouring libations or offerings, chosen deliberately over narrower jars to picture total, immediate outpouring rather than a slow trickle.
